routes.description: Establish a sufficiently reliable historical core of Jesus' death, the empty tomb, and postmortem appearances, then show that a bodily resurrection explains that combined evidence within a relevant theistic background framework.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical premises are adequately supported, the appearances are properly interpreted as bodily encounters, competing explanations lack comparable cumulative scope, and resurrection is rationally admissible given the relevant background evidence.

motionBridge.description: Connect the supported historical facts and comparative explanation to the conclusion that Jesus' bodily resurrection is rational.

centralBridges.description: Establish an early and sufficiently reliable source basis for the death, empty tomb, and reported appearances.
Show that the reported experiences and relevant texts concern bodily encounters rather than solely disembodied or private experiences.
Show that resurrection accounts for the combined evidence without requiring the unsupported conjunctions attributed to rival explanations.
Supply relevant background grounds under which resurrection is not excluded solely by ordinary expectations about death.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support actual death and an empty burial place as constraints on survival, vision-only, and body-removal accounts.
Use cumulative theistic or postmortem-awareness considerations only insofar as they bear on the antecedent plausibility of resurrection.

routes.description: Show that the partisan and incomplete historical record underdetermines what occurred, that nonphysical experiences or unknown body-removal scenarios remain available, and that a miracle conclusion requires background commitments not established by the reports alone.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the evidence cannot securely establish a publicly observable risen body, ordinary or unresolved alternatives remain live, or the prior theological requirements for identifying the event as divine resurrection are not independently warranted.

motionBridge.description: Connect evidential underdetermination and the demanding miracle standard to withholding a bodily-resurrection conclusion.

centralBridges.description: Establish that source dates, partisanship, eyewitness status, and limited independent corroboration restrict the warranted historical inference.
Preserve a reasonable interpretation of the reported experiences that does not establish tangible, publicly observable bodily encounters.
Show that psychological experiences, unknown removal scenarios, or other unresolved possibilities prevent a unique resurrection inference.
Require justified beliefs about a supernatural agent and its intentions before identifying an extraordinary report as a resurrection miracle.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether touching narratives and Pauline spiritual-body language actually establish bodily continuity and physical interaction.
Apply an evidential threshold appropriate to extraordinary perception and postmortem-awareness reports used to alter prior probability.

sections.title: Historical Sources and Early Testimony
sections.rationale: The reliability, dating, independence, and eyewitness connections of the surviving testimony determine what historical premises may enter either side's inference.

sections.title: Death, Burial, and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: Actual death and the condition of the burial place constrain survival, vision-only, body-removal, and resurrection accounts without alone deciding among them.

sections.title: Bodily Character of the Reported Appearances
sections.rationale: The motion specifically concerns bodily resurrection, making physical contact, group observation, Pauline terminology, and public corroboration a distinct burden-bearing issue.

sections.title: Naturalistic Alternatives and Explanatory Scope
sections.rationale: The comparative inference depends on whether grief visions, conversion phenomena, collective experiences, removal scenarios, or combinations of them explain the historical claims.

sections.title: Prior Probability and the Miracle Framework
sections.rationale: The rationality of accepting an extraordinary conclusion depends partly on how natural-law expectations, theistic background beliefs, and alleged postmortem evidence bear on prior plausibility.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Habermas identifies a broadly accepted historical core that includes Jesus' crucifixion, reported appearances, transformed disciples, and the conversions of James and Paul.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the discussion to Habermas, and the uninterrupted answer presents his historical-facts case.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the principal historical claims that the later explanatory argument is intended to interpret.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: As a constructive overview, it clearly identifies several relevant facts but supplies only compressed support for their acceptance.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical-core proposition is recoverable, though the breadth of scholarly acceptance varies among the listed facts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The passage invokes broad scholarly acceptance while only implicitly distinguishing the stronger and weaker consensus claims.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The listed facts form a coherent historical foundation, with the later explanatory bridge remaining outside this move.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt identifies a consensus-based factual core but does not document representativeness or defend each listed item.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central historical-foundation bridge and supplies several of its major factual premises.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive inventory does not substantially engage a developed opposing interpretation in this selected span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly lists the empty tomb, appearance experiences, transformation, early preaching, James, and Paul.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Uncertain dating, Christian partisanship, the Gospel writers' lack of eyewitness status, and the absence of independent Jerusalem testimony seriously limit the historical warrant supplied by the surviving sources.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Flew, whose first-person answer directly identifies the deficiencies he sees in the historical record.

components.text: Whether the asserted historical core rests on sources reliable enough to warrant treating its elements as historical facts.
Whether the several listed facts enjoy comparably broad scholarly acceptance rather than merely being asserted together.

response.rationale: Flew directly attacks source reliability through partisanship, eyewitness status, and missing independent Jerusalem corroboration, but does not separately examine the acceptance level of each fact.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the decisive source-reliability issue but leaves the item-by-item consensus claim largely untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source objection is clear, but the claim that all evidence is Christian and non-eyewitness is broader than the excerpt supports.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Categorical language about all surviving evidence exceeds the specific source limitations actually identified in the passage.

charity.alternative: Early partisan testimony may still preserve historically useful information and may incorporate eyewitness-linked traditions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Partisanship alone does not defeat testimony; the force depends on dating, dependence, and corroboration.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The limitations relevantly reduce confidence, though they do not by themselves entail that the reported core is unreliable.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific deficiencies are named, but their scope and the categorical characterization of the evidence are insufficiently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the con side's central source-limitations bridge with multiple express considerations.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection identifies genuine limitations but treats Christian provenance and nonautographic eyewitness status too nearly as wholesale defeat.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew cites Christian authorship, lack of direct eyewitness authorship, and no independent testimony from Jerusalem's wider population.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: The early tradition in First Corinthians 15 connects Paul with Peter and James and provides exceptionally early testimony from named eyewitnesses to reported appearances.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests an example, and Habermas gives a sustained first-person exposition of First Corinthians 15 and Galatians.

components.text: Whether the surviving testimony lacks sufficiently early, eyewitness-linked material to warrant the appearance reports.
Whether Christian partisanship independently limits the reliability of the Pauline tradition.
Whether independent non-Christian Jerusalem corroboration is absent.

response.rationale: Habermas answers the dating and eyewitness-link component with Paul, Peter, James, First Corinthians 15, and Galatians, while leaving partisanship and external corroboration unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply strongly contacts the decisive early-eyewitness component but does not answer two other material source objections.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim about an early Pauline tradition and named eyewitness links is clear, with transmission details somewhat compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The early dating is well connected to named figures, but direct derivation of the entire list from Peter and James remains inferential.

charity.alternative: An early creed linked to eyewitnesses can remain partisan, mediated testimony rather than independent confirmation of bodily events.
charity.decisiveQualification: Early transmission improves proximity but does not automatically establish independence, physicality, or accuracy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from early contact with Peter and James to early appearance testimony is coherent, with one transmission bridge implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named texts and persons provide specific support, though the sourcing of the formula and its independence remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply directly attacks the central source-limitations bridge at its early dating and eyewitness-link requirements.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly addresses proximity and eyewitness connection but does not incorporate the remaining independence qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt connects Paul with Peter and James and identifies their names within the First Corinthians 15 appearance list.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: The disciples' reported experiences can be interpreted as grief-related visions, while Paul's experience can be interpreted as a dramatic psychological religious conversion rather than observation of a risen body.
moves.attributionBasis: Flew is directly invited to explain the agreed experiences and gives both the grief-vision proposal and his psychological account of Paul.

components.text: Whether reported appearance experiences require an external risen body rather than psychologically generated experiences.
Whether the early Pauline tradition establishes bodily observation rather than merely an interpreted religious experience.
Whether transformation of the disciples and conversions of James and Paul favor resurrection over psychological explanations.

response.rationale: Flew offers grief visions for the disciples and a dramatic religious-conversion model for Paul, directly providing nonbodily interpretations of experience and transformation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the appearance and conversion phenomena, although its psychological mechanisms remain only sketched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alternative is clear, but Flew retreats from 'conversion psychosis' and does not delimit which disciples or reports it explains.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Flew presents psychological interpretations cautiously and expressly disclaims confidence in the moderator's stronger diagnostic label.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The alternatives are possible and internally compatible, but the inference lacks a developed mechanism covering the varied reports.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to familiar grief and conversion phenomena is relevant but supplies no representative evidence or detailed comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central nonbodily-interpretation bridge for both disciples and Paul.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage advances alternatives without materially characterizing or testing a developed resurrection explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly proposes grief hallucination for disciples and compares Paul's case to spectacular religious conversions.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Grief hallucinations do not jointly explain the reported group appearances, varied witnesses and settings, empty tomb, and lasting transformation of the disciples.
moves.attributionBasis: Habermas announces his transition to grief hallucinations and continues the same answer until the moderator solicits Flew's response.

components.text: Whether grief hallucinations can explain the reported range of witnesses, settings, group appearances, and subsequent transformation.
Whether a separate conversion experience adequately explains Paul's report.
Whether source partisanship and limited independent corroboration constrain the underlying reports.

response.rationale: Habermas directly challenges the psychological alternatives by citing varied people and circumstances, group scope, transformation, and the empty tomb, but does not answer the source objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive explanatory-scope problem while leaving documentation and some psychological comparison compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative objection is recoverable, but general claims about what hallucinations do and do not cause are insufficiently qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The varied-data challenge is forceful, but the generalization about hallucination and transformation receives limited support.

charity.alternative: Different psychological experiences could affect different witnesses, while an independent event accounts for the empty tomb.
charity.decisiveQualification: A combined alternative may be less simple without being impossible, and group reports require source-level scrutiny.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cumulative mismatch is a coherent objection, though plurality of phenomena does not itself exclude multiple psychological causes.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete categories of reports are named, but clinical generalizations and transformation claims rest on compressed authority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central alternative-underdetermination bridge by contesting the scope of its psychological account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes distinct people and circumstances but treats the alternative too uniformly and incompletely addresses combined explanations.

moves.evidenceBasis: Habermas invokes different people, locations, conditions, group reports, an empty tomb, and claimed lasting transformation.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: The severe shortage of non-Christian evidence leaves a broad background of historical ignorance, so the record cannot confidently establish what happened or warrant a publicly observable physical-resurrection account.
moves.attributionBasis: Flew answers the moderator's question in the first person and states the epistemic limits he believes the evidence imposes.

components.text: Whether early Christian testimony is sufficient to support confident conclusions about what physically occurred.
Whether the asserted historical core can be accepted confidently against a broad background of missing evidence.
Whether the cumulative objections to hallucination overcome the underlying source limitations.

response.rationale: Flew expressly argues that the shortage of non-Christian evidence prevents high confidence about the event, contacting the foundation claims but not the detailed anti-hallucination reasoning.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial response contacts the decisive epistemic sufficiency issue but remains general and does not examine the particular evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly limited to inability to reach conclusions with great confidence, rather than complete historical skepticism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cautious conclusion matches an argument from sparse corroboration and openly acknowledges the resulting uncertainty.

charity.alternative: Early Christian sources may still permit confident conclusions when independently early, multiply attested, or otherwise well explained.
charity.decisiveQualification: Scarcity of non-Christian material alone does not determine the reliability of the surviving evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Sparse corroboration rationally lowers confidence, though the degree of underdetermination requires source-specific analysis not supplied here.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The absence of non-Christian evidence is concrete, but the move does not assess the quality and independence of extant sources.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly connects evidential underdetermination to withholding the motion's bodily-resurrection conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response allows that there is evidence but gives too little consideration to methods for extracting warranted conclusions from sparse records.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew emphasizes the enormous shortage of non-Christian evidence and the broad historical ignorance surrounding the accepted list.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: The Thomas narrative reports sight and an invitation to touch but does not clearly report that Thomas actually touched Jesus, so it does not establish physical contact with a risen body.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Flew whether he accepts the four facts, and Flew personally develops the Thomas-based qualification to literal appearances.

components.text: Whether the reported appearances included clearly attested physical contact with a risen body.
Whether early Pauline appearance testimony establishes tangible bodily interaction.
Whether varied appearance reports collectively establish physical rather than visionary experiences.

response.rationale: The Thomas observation directly contacts one physical-contact narrative, but it does not answer the broader early Pauline or cumulative appearance evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts a secondary physical-text component but only partially addresses the broader bodily-appearance demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The narrow textual point is clearly and appropriately limited to the absence of an explicit report that Thomas touched Jesus.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Flew carefully says that as far as he can see the text does not report completed touching, matching the narrow warrant.

charity.alternative: The invitation to touch and Thomas's response may be intended narratively to establish bodily reality without reporting completed contact.
charity.decisiveQualification: Narrative implication is weaker than an explicit statement that Thomas actually touched Jesus.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between an invitation to touch and a report of actual touching is clear and logically material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The narrow textual claim is specifically grounded, though its implications for all physical encounter traditions are limited.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports the subsidiary physical-texts bridge through a focused textual qualification.

representationalCharity.rationale: The criticism fairly preserves the invitation while accurately isolating the missing report of completed physical contact.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes Jesus' instruction to touch from the narrative's failure expressly to say Thomas performed the act.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Johannine and Gospel testimony to touching, close observation, eating, and Jesus' denial that he was a spirit supports the claim that witnesses reported a literal physical resurrection body.
moves.attributionBasis: Habermas responds in the first person with a connected citation-based argument from First John and Luke about seeing and touching Jesus.

components.text: Whether Gospel and Johannine texts report physical interaction even if Thomas's completed touch is not expressly narrated.
Whether sparse and partisan sources justify treating the physical-interaction narratives as historical events.
Whether reported touching, eating, and close observation are compatible with a purely visionary account.

response.rationale: Habermas broadens the textual evidence beyond Thomas to touching, seeing, eating, and denial of being a spirit, but does not answer the historical-source reliability objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response contacts the decisive physical-text issue and the vision alternative, while leaving source warrant unaddressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The textual inference is clear, although the move sometimes shifts from what texts report to what witnesses historically did.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The texts support reported physicality, but the passage somewhat overstates the bridge from narrative testimony to established event.

charity.alternative: Physicalizing narratives may be later literary testimony and Thomas's actual touch remains unreported.
charity.decisiveQualification: Multiple physical motifs strengthen textual physicality without independently establishing their historical occurrence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Touching, eating, and denying spirit status coherently support a bodily reading, with historicity as a separate bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several specific textual features are supplied, but source dating, independence, and historical reliability are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central bodily-appearances bridge with multiple asserted physical-interaction motifs.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly goes beyond Thomas but does not preserve the distinction between textual representation and historical verification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites hands touching, Jesus inviting touch, denying ghostly status, eating, and repeated seeing and touching.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Paul's terminology and stated beliefs in First Corinthians 15 and Philippians 3 indicate bodily transformation and physical resurrection rather than a disembodied spirit.
moves.attributionBasis: After the break Habermas resumes his explicitly identified argument about Paul's understanding, continuing through the delivered boundary context.

components.text: Whether Paul's own terminology supplies evidence for a bodily rather than merely nonphysical resurrection conception.
Whether the Thomas narrative expressly records completed physical contact.
Whether Paul's experience is better understood as conversion psychology rather than encounter with a risen body.

response.rationale: Habermas supplies Pauline linguistic and textual evidence for bodily transformation, but it does not directly answer Thomas or establish the phenomenology of Paul's conversion experience.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response contacts the physical-interpretation issue but leaves other decisive experiential and source questions unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The body-versus-spirit contrast is recoverable, though the transliterated Greek terms and 'physical' require a more careful semantic distinction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Pauline body language supports embodied transformation, but the simple lexical contrast does not alone settle every sense of physical continuity.

charity.alternative: Paul's 'spiritual body' can denote transformed embodiment without implying an ordinary material body or identical appearance phenomenology.
charity.decisiveQualification: Embodiment and ordinary physical composition are distinct interpretive questions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The lexical and cross-textual argument is coherent, though it relies on an implicit equation of bodily transformation with physicality.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First Corinthians and Philippians provide specific evidence, but the linguistic warrant and competing exegesis are underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central bodily-appearances bridge through Paul's conception of resurrection embodiment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes transformation but compresses the strongest semantic qualification concerning what kind of body Paul envisages.

moves.evidenceBasis: Habermas contrasts pneuma with soma and invokes First Corinthians 15 and Philippians 3 as evidence of bodily transformation.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Describing a body as spiritual or immaterial does not identify bodily characteristics and therefore does not by itself provide a coherent account of a genuinely physical resurrection body.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly invites Flew to answer, and the ensuing first-person response is continuous until the next question.

components.text: Whether calling the resurrection body spiritual coherently identifies a genuinely bodily and physical mode of existence.
Whether touching, eating, and observation texts independently support a physical encounter.

response.rationale: Flew directly contests the conceptual intelligibility of a spiritual or immaterial body, but does not address the separate Gospel evidence of touching and eating.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the Pauline conceptual issue but leaves the independent physical-encounter evidence unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is recoverable, but it treats 'spiritual' and 'immaterial' as equivalent without establishing that Pauline usage.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion that an immaterial substance is nothing and a spiritual body no body exceeds the semantic premise offered.

charity.alternative: A spiritual body may mean a body transformed or governed by spirit rather than an immaterial nonentity.
charity.decisiveQualification: The Pauline adjective need not negate embodiment or identify composition as immaterial.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference works only if spiritual means wholly immaterial, a central equivocation not defended in the passage.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual intuition is asserted without textual or linguistic support for the decisive equivalence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the subsidiary physical-texts challenge to Pauline spiritual-body language.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection materially weakens the strongest embodied reading by assuming the contested equivalence between spiritual and immaterial.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew equates spiritual with immaterial and argues that immateriality supplies no bodily characteristic or substance.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: What it is rational to conclude from an alleged miracle depends on prior beliefs, so the same report may rationally support resurrection for a believer while leaving a skeptic rationally suspecting error.
moves.attributionBasis: Habermas asks Flew directly what he thinks, and Flew answers in the first person while contrasting his outlook with Jewish and Christian priors.

components.text: Whether bodily-resurrection evidence can rationally compel the same conclusion independently of antecedent worldview commitments.
Whether extraordinary physical-encounter reports overcome a skeptic's expectation of mistake.
Whether the historical core alone warrants a miracle conclusion.

response.rationale: Flew directly argues that rational interpretation of all such reports depends on prior beliefs, applying this to believers and skeptics rather than disputing each textual detail.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive inferential bridge from reports to miracle, though it does not specify how priors should be justified or updated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dependence claim is clearly framed as a contrast in rational response conditional on different prior beliefs.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim appropriately allows different rational responses and acknowledges that an apparent miracle may involve mistake.

charity.alternative: Sufficiently strong historical evidence might rationally overwhelm initially skeptical priors.
charity.decisiveQualification: Prior dependence does not imply that posterior judgments are immune to common evidence or rational updating.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional dependence of extraordinary inference on priors is coherent, though it does not by itself vindicate either prior.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Bayesian-style point is plausible but remains conceptual, without defending the skeptic's actual error probability.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly establishes the con side's central miracle-background requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly notes prior dependence but leaves the evidence's potential likelihood ratio and updating force underdeveloped.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew expressly contrasts the rational response of a prior believer with his own suspicion of error when facing an apparent miracle.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Jesus' death by crucifixion is supported by medical considerations, critical consensus, non-Christian sources, Pauline testimony, and the failure of survival scenarios.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Habermas for sources, and the response identifies scholarly, medical, extra-biblical, and Pauline grounds in an extended answer.

components.text: Whether Jesus' death has sufficiently varied support beyond partisan Christian narrative sources.
Whether the sparse ancient record permits confident conclusions at least about death by crucifixion.
Whether establishing death materially changes the prior probability of miraculous resurrection.

response.rationale: Habermas directly supplies medical, critical, extra-biblical, and Pauline grounds for death, answering source scarcity for this premise but not the later miracle inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response explicitly contacts the decisive evidential demand for actual death through several asserted lines of support.

precisionFindings.rationale: The death claim and its support categories are clear, though 'wide variety' and consensus strength are loosely specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Death by crucifixion is strongly supported within the record, but near-certainty rests partly on compressed authority and unspecified sources.

charity.alternative: Sparse ancient evidence may still leave some uncertainty about death details or survival scenarios.
charity.decisiveQualification: Multiple source types and the ordinary lethality of crucifixion can make death much better supported than later resurrection claims.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The convergence of medical, historical, non-Christian, and Pauline considerations coherently supports actual death.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Multiple specific support categories are supplied, though individual extra-biblical sources and medical warrants are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the subsidiary death-and-tomb bridge at its actual-death requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response accurately distinguishes a well-supported ordinary event from the record's more contested extraordinary implications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The passage cites medical data, critical scholarship, extra-biblical evidence, named skeptical scholars, Paul, and failed survival accounts.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: The empty tomb is supported by early accounts, hostile acknowledgment, proclamation in Jerusalem, and the counterproductive identification of women as its primary witnesses.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests the grounds for an empty tomb, and Habermas gives a numbered, continuous set of historical considerations before inviting Flew's response.

components.text: Whether the empty tomb has multiple early or otherwise probative grounds beyond unsupported Christian assertion.
Whether the available record permits a confident conclusion that the burial place was empty.
Whether an empty tomb itself warrants identifying a miracle.

response.rationale: Habermas answers the tomb's historical support through early accounts, hostile acknowledgment, Jerusalem proclamation, and women witnesses, without claiming that emptiness alone proves a miracle.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response expressly contacts the tomb-evidence demand through a cumulative set of considerations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative proposition is clear, but 'the Jews admitted' compresses distinct, later reports into a broad hostile-witness claim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Several relevant indicators are presented, while independence and dating of hostile acknowledgment receive insufficient qualification.

charity.alternative: Later hostile explanations and women-witness traditions may derive from Christian narratives rather than independent confirmation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hostile acknowledgment and embarrassment have force only after dependence, dating, and cultural assumptions are defended.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The considerations coherently converge on emptiness, though none independently excludes dependence or later development.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named texts and argumentative features are provided, but independence, chronology, and the women-witness warrant remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the subsidiary death-and-tomb bridge by defending the empty burial place.

representationalCharity.rationale: The cumulative case recognizes several evidential types but compresses the strongest dependence and transmission qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Habermas cites Acts 13, First Corinthians 15, Matthew, Justin Martyr, Tertullian, Jerusalem proclamation, and women witnesses.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Even if the tomb was empty, the absence of independent witnesses leaves many possible ways the body could have been removed, and the available ancient evidence cannot satisfactorily reconstruct what occurred.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Flew what happened to the body, and Flew answers in the first person while expressly declining to offer a definite reconstruction.

components.text: Whether establishing an empty tomb uniquely supports resurrection rather than unresolved removal scenarios.
Whether Jesus actually died before the body disappeared.
Whether the empty tomb itself is historically established by sufficiently independent witnesses.

response.rationale: Flew accepts the issue conditionally and argues that missing independent witnesses and numerous removal possibilities block reconstruction, while not disputing death.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive underdetermination demand but offers possible removal only generically rather than as a supported account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly claims underdetermination rather than asserting a particular removal theory and expressly declines reconstruction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that many removal possibilities remain is calibrated to the acknowledged lack of reconstructive evidence.

charity.alternative: The cumulative empty-tomb evidence may make removal accounts less plausible even without modern witnesses or cameras.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mere logical possibilities do not carry equal explanatory weight without motive, opportunity, and evidential fit.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Lack of independent observation coherently supports underdetermination, but possible removal alone does not establish competitive probability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The evidential gap is identified, while the purported range of removal scenarios remains wholly unspecified and unsupported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central alternative-underdetermination bridge through unresolved body-removal possibilities.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly avoids inventing a theory but does not compare the generic removal possibility with the specific cumulative case.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew cites no independent witnesses, notes multiple possible ways to remove a body, and refuses an unsupported definite reconstruction.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Combining distinct hallucination accounts for Paul and the disciples with an unexplained removal of the body compounds unsupported assumptions rather than producing a coherent explanation of the combined evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly turns to Habermas and asks him to survey naturalistic alternatives, which he does through a sustained first-person analysis.

components.text: Whether an unspecified removal possibility provides a coherent explanation when combined with the reported appearances and transformations.
Whether separate hallucination or conversion explanations adequately cover both disciples and Paul.
Whether source scarcity prevents comparative assessment of the combined alternatives.
Whether the underlying appearance and transformation reports are independently reliable.

response.rationale: Habermas directly tests the conjunction of stolen or removed body, appearance explanations, and transformation, but leaves the source-level objections untreated.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive combined-explanation problem while not answering the reliability of the data being combined.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative comparison is recoverable, but claims about disciple martyrdom and the failure of all combined alternatives are broadly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conjunction-cost argument is relevant, but the passage does not quantify or thoroughly compare the assumptions on either side.

charity.alternative: Different causes may explain distinct facts, and an explanation need not be a single mechanism if the evidence itself is heterogeneous.
charity.decisiveQualification: Conjunction costs matter, but resurrection also requires substantial historical and background assumptions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Combining independent speculative accounts can reduce explanatory economy, though complexity alone does not make the conjunction false.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several data points and alternatives are named, but martyrdom, transformation, theft, and hallucination warrants remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central comparative-explanation bridge by challenging the scope and economy of combined rivals.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply identifies fragmentation in the alternatives but does not symmetrically examine the assumptions required by its preferred explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Habermas combines Gospel, Pauline, and extra-biblical claims with transformation, body theft, and hallucination alternatives.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Background evidence for God's existence, present-day divine action, and survival after death can raise the antecedent probability of resurrection beyond that supplied by ordinary experience alone.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly invites Habermas to answer, and the sustained first-person response develops his explicitly theistic approach.

components.text: Whether there are independent background considerations capable of raising resurrection's antecedent probability.
Whether background theism resolves the historical uncertainty concerning body removal.
Whether background evidence repairs the sparse historical record.

response.rationale: Habermas accepts the relevance of priors and proposes evidence for God, divine action, and postmortem survival, but does not supply that evidence within the selected move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response contacts the decisive prior-probability component but largely announces rather than executes the background case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clearly conditional on additional worldview evidence and explicitly notes that those subjects exceed this debate's scope.
